# Error Handling, Logging, and Observability {#sec-error-handling}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A streaming engine cannot fail silently. A query that produces
wrong answers is worse than a query that crashes. NebulaStream
treats error handling as a first-class concern: there is a
written design document for it
(`docs/design/20240711_error_handling.md`), a centralised
exception list, two assertion macros for invariants, and a
discipline of distinguishing recoverable errors from bugs.

This chapter walks through the discipline.

---

## 17.1 Bugs vs. errors {#sec-bugs-vs-errors}

The first useful distinction is also the bluntest: some failures
are bugs (the code is wrong) and some are errors (the world is
wrong). They warrant different handling.

A **bug** is a violation of an invariant the code maintains. The
worker dequeued a task whose pipeline weak_ptr was supposed to be
non-null but is null. The hash map's `getNumberOfTuples` returned
a value larger than its capacity. These are facts about the code's
internal consistency that, if violated, mean the code has a defect
the user cannot work around. The right response is to fail loudly
and crash; continuing is dangerous.

An **error** is an external condition the code anticipated. The
file source was given a path that does not exist. A field in the
input failed to parse as `UINT64`. The TCP source's connection
dropped mid-stream. These are facts about the world the engine has
no control over. The right response is to handle them — either
recover, or report a clean error to the user.

NebulaStream uses different mechanisms for the two:

- **Bugs**: `INVARIANT` and `PRECONDITION` macros. Crash on
  violation.
- **Errors**: typed exceptions. Throw on unrecoverable failure;
  return `std::expected<T, Exception>` or `std::optional<T>` for
  expected-but-unsuccessful outcomes.

We will see each.

---

## 17.2 The exception list: one file, eighty types {#sec-exception-list}

NebulaStream has a single file that defines every exception type
it can throw. The file is
`nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc`. Each entry uses an
`EXCEPTION` macro:

```cpp
// nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc (sketch)
EXCEPTION(InvalidConfigParameter, 1000, "Invalid configuration parameter")
EXCEPTION(CannotLoadConfig, 1001, "Cannot load configuration file")
// ... ~80 more entries ...
EXCEPTION(InvalidQuerySyntax, 2000, "Invalid query syntax")
EXCEPTION(UnknownSourceType, 2017, "Unknown source type")
EXCEPTION(QueryCompilerError, 2032, "Query compiler error")
EXCEPTION(BufferAllocationFailure, 3000, "Buffer allocation failed")
EXCEPTION(QueryNotRegistered, 3001, "Query not registered")
EXCEPTION(ArithmeticalError, 3013, "Arithmetic error")
EXCEPTION(CannotConnectToCoordinator, 5000, "Cannot connect to coordinator")
EXCEPTION(InternalErrorAssert, 9000, "Internal error - assertion violated")
EXCEPTION(FunctionNotImplemented, 9001, "Function not implemented")
```

Three observations.

**Centralisation.** Every exception is in this file. New
exception types are added here and only here. The CLAUDE.md
guideline is explicit: "All exception types defined in a single
file." This is unusual — most C++ codebases scatter exception
definitions across translation units — and it is unusually
useful: you can grep one file to know everything that can go
wrong.

**Numeric codes by category.** The four-digit codes group
exceptions by error class. The verified taxonomy as of
`origin/main` is:

| Range | Count | Category | Representative codes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1XXX | 5 | Configuration | InvalidConfigParameter (1000), CannotLoadConfig (1001) |
| 2XXX | 38 | Query parsing / compilation | InvalidQuerySyntax (2000), QueryCompilerError (2032), InvalidOptimizerRuleset (2037) |
| **23XX** | **4** | **Distributed** (sub-block of 2XXX) | PlacementFailure (2300), InvalidTopology (2301), UnknownWorker (2302), DistributedFailure (2303) |
| 3XXX | 8 | Runtime | BufferAllocationFailure (3000), ArithmeticalError (3013) |
| 4XXX | 5 | Sources / sinks | CannotFormatSourceData (4000), CannotOpenSink (4004) |
| 5XXX | 6 | API | QueryNotFound (5000), QueryStatusFailed (5005) |
| 9XXX | 4 | Internal bugs | FunctionNotImplemented (9000), InvalidDynamicCast (9002) |
| 9999 / 10000 | 2 | Special | UnknownException, TestException |

**Total: 70 exception types**, all defined in one file. A
user-visible error message includes the code; an operator
seeing `error 4004: Cannot open sink` can distinguish "the
output path is bad" from `error 2300: Placement failure`
("the ILP solver could not place this query").

The 23XX block is worth calling out separately. Distributed
deployments (Chapter 19) introduce four error modes — the ILP
fails, a topology cycle is detected, an unknown worker is
referenced, or a worker-side failure propagates to the
coordinator. They live as a sub-block of 2XXX rather than
their own range because, conceptually, all four are
"compilation/registration" failures: they happen before or
during query startup, not during steady-state execution. The
5XXX network range covers in-flight network errors.

**Structured construction.** The `EXCEPTION` macro generates a
constructor that supports `fmt::format`-style formatting:

```cpp
// (Sketch of what EXCEPTION expands to)
inline Exception InvalidConfigParameter() {
    return Exception("Invalid configuration parameter", 1000);
}
inline Exception InvalidConfigParameter(std::string msg) {
    return Exception(fmt::format("Invalid configuration parameter; {}\n", msg), 1000);
}
template <typename... Args>
inline Exception InvalidConfigParameter(fmt::format_string<Args...> fmt_msg, Args&&... args) {
    return Exception(
        fmt::format("Invalid configuration parameter; {}\n",
                    fmt::format(fmt_msg, std::forward<Args>(args)...)),
        1000);
}
```

`throw InvalidConfigParameter("port {} is out of range", 99999)`
produces a message that the caller can format and the user can
read.

## 17.3 INVARIANT and PRECONDITION {#sec-invariant-macros}

For bugs, NebulaStream uses two macros, both in
`nes-common/include/ErrorHandling.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-common/include/ErrorHandling.hpp
#define INVARIANT(condition, formatString, ...)                                \
    do {                                                                        \
        if (!(condition)) {                                                    \
            auto trace = cpptrace::generate_trace().to_string(true);           \
            NES_ERROR("Invariant violated: ({}): " formatString "\n\n{}",      \
                      #condition __VA_OPT__(, ) __VA_ARGS__, trace);           \
            if (auto logger = ::NES::Logger::getInstance())                    \
                logger->shutdown();                                            \
            std::terminate();                                                  \
        }                                                                      \
    } while (false)
```

`INVARIANT(condition, fmt, args…)` checks a condition that should
be true if the engine's logic is correct. On violation, it
produces a stack trace via cpptrace, logs at ERROR level, flushes
the logger, and terminates. There is no recovery path; the engine
crashes.

`PRECONDITION` is the symmetric macro for function entry: a
condition the caller is supposed to ensure. Same mechanics, same
crash-on-violation behaviour.

Both macros are compiled away in `Release` and `Benchmark` builds
(via `#define NO_ASSERT`). In `Debug` and `RelWithDebInfo`, they
fire. The reasoning is conventional: production should not pay
the cost of internal-consistency checks; development should pay
the cost generously.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.1: when INVARIANT fires"}
A worker thread dequeues a `WorkTask` and locks its weak_ptr
to a `RunningQueryPlanNode`. The lock fails (returns nullptr).
The worker logs and drops the task — that is graceful, not a
bug. But suppose the worker's *own state* says it should have a
non-null pointer at this point: the worker just locked a
weak_ptr two lines up and stored the result, and now the result
is nullptr. That would be:

```cpp
INVARIANT(strongRef != nullptr,
          "RunningQueryPlanNode disappeared mid-handler for query {}",
          task.queryId);
```

If this fires, something has destroyed the node while a worker
held a strong reference to it — which the engine's lifecycle
machinery should make impossible. The crash is correct: the
alternative is undefined behaviour.
:::

## 17.4 Logging through spdlog {#sec-logging}

NebulaStream uses spdlog [@spdlog] as its logger. Configuration
lives in
`nes-single-node-worker/src/SingleNodeWorker.cpp` and the API is
the standard `NES_TRACE`, `NES_DEBUG`, `NES_INFO`, `NES_WARN`,
`NES_ERROR` macros. fmt-style formatting is the convention:

```cpp
NES_INFO("Query {} registered with {} pipelines",
         queryId, plan.getPipelines().size());
```

The build-type-aware default log levels (from CLAUDE.md):

| Build type | Default level |
|---|---|
| Debug | TRACE |
| RelWithDebInfo | WARN |
| Release | ERROR |
| Benchmark | (no logging) |

The benchmark build strips logging entirely at compile time —
even an unreached `NES_TRACE` call is gone. This is the right
choice for performance experiments where each remaining cycle
matters; it is the wrong default for production debugging, which
is why production typically uses Release rather than Benchmark.

There is also a custom **GoogleEventTracePrinter** that, when
enabled, writes Chrome-tracing-compatible JSON for the worker.
You can drag the resulting trace into `chrome://tracing` and
visualise the worker's activity at sub-millisecond granularity.
This is one of the engine's better debugging aids and is a
standard tool we will use throughout Chapter 21 (benchmarking).

## 17.5 Recoverable errors: the std::expected pattern {#sec-expected-pattern}

Some errors are not exceptional in the "should never happen"
sense — they are routine. The user submits a query that fails to
parse. A source's file path is wrong. The right response is not
"throw and unwind", it is "return the error to the caller."

NebulaStream uses `std::expected<T, Exception>` for these cases.
The query-registration path returns one:

```cpp
// nes-single-node-worker/src/SingleNodeWorker.cpp (sketch)
std::expected<QueryId, Exception>
SingleNodeWorker::registerQuery(LogicalPlan plan) noexcept
{
    if (plan.getQueryId() == INVALID_QUERY_ID) {
        std::uniform_int_distribution<size_t> dist(
            QueryId::INITIAL,
            std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max());
        plan.setQueryId(QueryId(dist(*idGenerator.wlock())));
    }
    auto request = std::make_unique<QueryCompilation::QueryCompilationRequest>(plan);
    auto result = compiler->compileQuery(std::move(request));
    // returns std::expected<QueryId, Exception>
}
```

The function is `noexcept` and returns either a `QueryId` (success)
or an `Exception` (a typed error from the exception list). The
caller decides how to respond — typically by translating the
exception into a gRPC status code for the client.

This pattern keeps the *normal* flow visible — the function
signature reads "either I return a QueryId or I report an error"
— while keeping bugs (which use exceptions or terminate) clearly
distinct.

## 17.6 Distributed failure modes {#sec-distributed-failures}

The four 23XX exception types we catalogued in
@sec-exception-list cover specific failure shapes the
distributed layer can produce.

**`PlacementFailure` (2300).** The ILP solver returned no
feasible solution. Causes: a sink was declared on a worker
that has no path to the source's worker; a query asks for
more capacity than any single worker can provide; the user
declared sources and sinks that the topology cannot connect.
The exception travels back to the user as a registration error
(the query never starts).

**`InvalidTopology` (2301).** Adding a worker would create a
cycle in the DAG. Thrown by `NetworkTopology::addNode` (Chapter
19). This is a structural violation, not a runtime failure;
the offending registration is rejected and the catalog stays
consistent.

**`UnknownWorker` (2302).** The catalog was queried for a host
that was never registered. Usually a programming error in the
coordinator code; less commonly, a race between worker
deregistration and a placement decision that referenced the
worker. Either way, the engine cannot proceed safely — bare
hosts have no associated `WorkerConfig`, so it is unsafe to
guess.

**`DistributedFailure` (2303).** The catch-all for worker-side
errors that propagate up. A worker reports a runtime exception
to the coordinator; the coordinator wraps it in a
`DistributedFailure` carrying the original exception's
information. The user sees the coordinator's wrapped error;
the worker's logs carry the original.

What is *not* a 23XX exception: a transient network
disruption. If a worker becomes unreachable mid-query, the
coordinator's `DistributedQueryStatusSnapshot` flips
`hasConnectionException` and the global query status moves to
`Unreachable` (Chapter 19). This is a state, not an exception
— the engine does not throw on its own polling.

The asymmetry between "failed loud" (an exception) and "fell
silent" (`Unreachable`) is intentional. Loud failures are
problems the engine has identified; silent ones are situations
the engine cannot conclude about. Forcing the second into the
first would lose information.

## 17.7 Observability: where to look when something is wrong {#sec-observability}

Practical advice for the reader who has just hit an error in
NebulaStream:

1. **Check the log first.** The error code in the message lets
   you grep `nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc` for the
   declaration; the surrounding text usually points at the code
   path that failed.
2. **Run with `--logging.level=TRACE`.** TRACE is generous; it
   logs every task, every pipeline transition, every state
   change. For non-trivial bugs the answer is somewhere in the
   trace.
3. **Run in INTERPRETER mode.** If the bug might be in the JIT,
   `--worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER`
   removes the entire compilation pipeline and runs the trace
   directly. If the bug disappears, the bug is in code generation.
4. **Run with sanitizers.** The CLAUDE.md notes the CI builds
   matrix includes ASan, UBSan, and TSan. For
   memory-corruption-shaped bugs, a sanitizer build localises
   the bug almost instantly.
5. **Use the Chrome trace.** Enable `GoogleEventTracePrinter` and
   drag the JSON into `chrome://tracing` for a visual timeline.

The engine has invested visibly in observability. Most stream
engines' debug stories are worse.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch17-summary}

NebulaStream distinguishes bugs (handled by `INVARIANT`/
`PRECONDITION` macros that crash on violation) from recoverable
errors (handled by typed exceptions or `std::expected`). The
exception list is centralised in a single `.inc` file with
~80 typed exceptions organised into numeric ranges by category.
Logging is through spdlog with build-type-aware default levels,
and an optional Chrome-tracing-compatible event printer for
visualising worker activity. The discipline is to crash
forcefully on bug-shaped failures and recover gracefully on
world-shaped failures, with the line between the two made
visible by the choice of mechanism.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch17-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 17.1: cause an exception"}
Submit a query with an unknown source type:

```sql
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR demo TYPE InvalidType SET();
```

You should see an `UnknownSourceType` exception (code 2017).
Where in the binder is the type validated? Trace through the
function from the binding error to the user-visible message.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 17.2: trip an INVARIANT"}
Find a place in the codebase that calls `INVARIANT` with a
condition you can intentionally violate (e.g., a debug-only
sanity check). In a debug build, modify the surrounding code to
violate it. Run a query. The engine should crash with a stack
trace. The exit is intentional and informative — that is the
whole point of `INVARIANT`.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 17.3: chrome tracing"}
Enable `GoogleEventTracePrinter` (look for the configuration
option in the worker's startup code). Run a join systest. Drag
the resulting JSON file into `chrome://tracing`. Identify the
worker threads, the per-task durations, the gaps between tasks
(when the worker is idle).
:::
